In order to receive this award, a governmental unit must publish a budget document that meets program criteria as a policy document, as an operations guide, as a financial plan and as a communications device. The award is valid for a period of one year only. This is the 29th consecutive year the City has earned the award. We believe our current budget continues to conform to program requirements. ........................................................................................... 277 iv | City of Fremont FY 2026/27 Adopted Operating Budget Guide to the Document The budget is both a spending plan for the City’s available financial resources and the legal authority for City departments to spend the resources for public purposes. Through these resources, services are provided to meet the needs of Fremont residents. The City Council and City staff respond to the community’s needs in part through the budget. It balances not only revenues and costs, but also community priorities and interests. Accessibility Information This document does not meet the requirements of Department of Justice regulations for Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). However, efforts have been made to structure many of the tables for screen-reader compatibility. When using a screen-reader with financial tables please note: • A hyphen “-” represents zero • Negative numbers are shown in parenthesis Document Organization Budget Overview The City Manager’s Budget Overview sets the context for budget decisions by describing community and economic conditions affecting the budget. It outlines major initiatives underway and opportunities and challenges for the coming year. Summary Information This section of the document presents an overall picture of the City and the budget. It includes an organization chart, a description of the community, summary financial tables, a summary of citywide staffing changes associated with the budget, and documentation of the City’s compliance with State statutes and City policies regarding total expenditures and debt. This section also presents the City’s budget principles, a summary of departmental performance measures, and a summary of departmental objectives in a table that shows the alignment of objectives with citywide goals. General Fund Local government budgets are organized by funds in order to segregate and account for restricted resources. Each fund is a separate accounting entity. The General Fund provides the majority of resources for most of the services cities typically deliver, including the public safety, maintenance, and general government functions required to support direct services to the community. This section provides an analytical overview of the General Fund for the budget year. This section also places the budget in context with the financial forecast and provides a five-year historical review of General Fund sources and uses. Guide to the Document Other Funds The Other Funds section contains information regarding non-General Fund sources of revenue. These funds are grouped into Cost Centers and Internal Service, Special Revenue, and Capital categories. Internal Service funds are cost allocation mechanisms and, along with Cost Center funds, are proprietary in nature. Special Revenue funds and Capital funds are grouped with the General Fund and Debt Service funds and are described as “governmental funds.” The distinction between how the budgeted resources are accounted for in proprietary funds as compared to governmental funds is discussed in the “Basis of Budgetary Accounting” located in the Policies and Practices section of the document. A description and financial summary is provided for each category of Other Funds within the budget. Capital Budget Summary The Capital Improvement Program (CIP) is adopted biennially and includes appropriations for projects for Fiscal Years 2025/26 through 2026/27. Selected excerpts from the CIP are included with the operating budget to present a comprehensive picture of all the funds of the City and to reflect fund transfers between other operating funds and capital funds. This section contains a description of the CIP funds, a summary of budgeted expenditures by program category, and highlights of key projects. Department Budgets The majority of the budget document presents information on departmental budgets. Each departmental section provides the following information: • Department Mission Statement • Department Major Services - The purpose of this information is to give the reader an understanding of the scope of each department’s major service areas. • Department Overview - A summary of each department’s ongoing day-to-day core services and responsibilities. • Accomplishment Highlights - A list that highlights a few of the department’s most noteworthy accomplishments. • Objectives - A list of significant departmental objectives or one-time projects aligned with the City Council’s priorities that help to achieve departmental goals outside the day-to-day services provided by the department. • Performance Measurement - Information on performance measures and targets. • Sources of Funding - This information is in graphic form and illustrates the funds from which departments receive financial resources. Interfund transfers (to the General Fund) cover administrative department costs for services that are provided by the General Fund. This contribution is shown on the charts as “overhead charges to other funds.” Guide to the Document • Staffing - A historical staffing graph shows the level of staffing for each department. In addition, an organization chart displays individual positions and titles. • Expenditure Summary - This table shows the salary and benefits, operating, and capital costs associated with the department for the fiscal year. It also provides historical information and trends of previous funding levels. Departments comprised of multiple, discrete service areas also present a table summarizing their activities by those major service areas. • Major Budget Changes - A description of the major budget changes is included that compares the previous year’s budget with that for the current year. The major changes narrative includes any changes in salaries, benefits, and staffing. In addition, it describes operating, capital, and indirect expense allocation changes, but only if they vary by 5% up or down from the previous year. Staffing This section contains a summary of authorized positions by department and provides perspective on workforce trends. Policies and Glossary This section details the City’s budget and financial policies, and includes a glossary of budget terminology. Resolutions This section contains resolutions approving and adopting the City budget and the appropriation limit for the fiscal year. Guide to the Document This page intentionally left blank to facilitate double-sided printing Budget Overview Letter of Transmittal Honorable Mayor and Members of the City Council: Our City is committed to strong fiscal stewardship, transparency, and accountability over taxpayer dollars. Working together, the City Council and City staff ensure our budget and financial policies reflect the community’s priorities. Consistent with the City Council’s foundational principle of fiscal sustainability, General Fund budgeted expenditures for the coming year of $289.1 million have been limited to fit within the projected ongoing resources without the use of the Budget Uncertainty Reserve. Although projected revenue growth is sufficient to maintain staffing and services at their current levels, it does not provide capacity to restore the $3.2 million of ongoing maintenance support that was eliminated to balance the FY 2025/26 adopted budget or the $3.1 million of ongoing personnel, supplies, and services reductions that were needed to rebalance the FY 2025/26 budget after labor negotiations concluded. The adopted budget continues to incorporate the City Council’s and community’s highest priorities by maintaining funding for economic development, reducing homelessness, and ensuring public safety. In this message, I will highlight the following: • FY 2026/27 Fiscal Outlook • Economic Update • Key Budget Assumptions • Discussion of Unmet Needs • Major City Initiatives Budget Overview FY 2026/27 Fiscal Outlook Staff anticipates that the local economy will grow modestly during FY 2026/27 and total General Fund ongoing resources (revenues and transfers in) of $291.0 million are projected to increase by 3.0% over estimated actual ongoing resources in FY 2025/26. Property tax and sales tax are the City’s most significant revenue sources. Property tax revenues are estimated to total $152.5 million in FY 2025/26, and staff projects those revenues will increase to $158.2 million in FY 2026/27, an increase of 3.7%. The estimated increase in secured property value for FY 2026/27 is based on the California Consumer Price Index, property transfer tax data for calendar year 2025 and preliminary information from the County Assessor. High mortgage rates continue to reduce the number of home sales to historically low levels. With two quarters of available data, we are estimating FY 2025/26 sales tax revenue of $67.3 million and projecting FY 2026/27 sales tax revenue of $69.1 million, a 2.7% increase. Although the total revenue over the first two quarters is higher than anticipated, the State is investigating suspected sales tax misallocations by businesses which could be temporarily inflating our revenue numbers. Backing out an estimate for potentially misallocated revenue, we can still see underlying year-overyear growth of close to 3%. Business taxes are projected to yield $14.9 million in FY 2025/26. While this represents a 13.8% increase from the prior year, much of the gain results from several large payments we’ve received in the construction-related business tax revenue category along with a delayed payment attributable to FY 2024/25. The FY 2026/27 business tax estimate of $15.1 million assumes historical growth in the general business tax category and a continuation of construction activity at the current level. Hotel/motel occupancy tax revenues are estimated to total $6.9 million in FY 2025/26 and increase to $7.3 million in FY 2026/27. The strong growth in the current year estimate reflects one-time impacts from the Super Bowl in February 2026 and the World Cup in June 2026. The FY 2026/27 projection assumes growth returns to the most recent three-year average. The FY 2026/27 adopted operating budget maintains the General Fund Contingency Reserve at 16.7% of budgeted expenditures and transfers out, or $48.3 million, a level consistent with City Council policy and the recommended practice of the Government Finance Officers Association of the United States and Canada. The General Fund Budget Uncertainty Reserve is projected to end FY 2025/26 at $4.3 million. Budget Overview Economic Update The national economy is expected to continue expanding at a moderate rate. The Federal Reserve anticipates growth in the low 2% range in 2026 and 2027. Calendar year 2025 saw the national economy expand at a healthy 2.1% annual rate, but down from 2.8% in calendar year 2024. While the volatile path of tariff policy contributed to that slowdown, consumer spending consistently offset reductions in other areas of the economy as businesses hesitated to increase hiring or expand production. The advance estimate for the first quarter of 2026 reports that gross domestic product (GDP) increased by 2.0%. The employment situation has remained stable, with the April 2026 unemployment rate of 4.3% the same as March, just slightly down from February, and consistent with reported levels over the last year. The reluctance of businesses to expand or add staff in the face of the evolving global trade environment, combined with the potential for artificial intelligence to replace certain job types, has led to what some have characterized as a “no-hire, no-fire” labor market. Inflation has remained somewhat elevated throughout the past year, with the Federal Reserve’s preferred measure remaining at or close to 3% compared with its 2% target. However, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz at the end of February, following the commencement of military actions against Iran, immediately led to a jump in gasoline and fuel prices which is now just beginning to contribute to higher costs for goods and services. The press release from the most recent meeting of the Federal Reserve Open Market Committee on April 29th notes that: “Developments in the Middle East are contributing to a high level of uncertainty about the economic outlook.” Given the probability of elevated inflation over the next several months, if not longer, the Federal Reserve is unlikely to cut its interest rate target from the current level until the end of 2026 or early 2027. With no change in monetary policy, 30-year mortgage rates are expected to remain above 6% for the foreseeable future. The City’s revenue forecast assumes the economy will continue to grow at a moderate pace, supporting modest revenue growth for sales tax and business tax, but that continued high mortgage rates and interest rates will suppress property sales and development activity at least through the end of 2026. On a cautionary note, global oil and gas supply disruptions continuing into FY 2026/27 would increase the likelihood of an economic slowdown or possibly a recession. If that were to occur, staff would return to the City Council with recommendations for any necessary budget adjustments. Budget Overview Unmet Needs Fremont is a great place to live, work and do business. However, like many cities throughout California, our City faces long-term fiscal challenges that impact the City’s ability to maintain quality of life services at the level residents want and deserve. Important quality of life services we must continue to protect, maintain and improve include: • Police/Fire protection and emergency response services • Garbage and recycling services • Maintaining public parks • Streets/Roads repair • Protecting the safety of drivers, bikers, and pedestrians. We continue to grapple with increasing needs for public safety services and the growing cost of maintaining Fremont’s roads and other infrastructure. The construction of new residential units as well as commercial and industrial development throughout the City is necessitating increased police and fire response to protect public safety. The majority of Fremont’s public infrastructure was constructed many years ago and now requires either an increased level or increased frequency of repairs, compounded by not having had adequate resources to spend on maintenance in the past. Moreover, as Fremont continues to grow, additional infrastructure is added that must be maintained, further stretching the City’s limited maintenance resources. Finally, new requirements result in increased costs. Some of these requirements are voluntary, such as the City’s commitment to improving traffic and pedestrian safety and traffic congestion, and encouraging alternative forms of transportation, through implementation of the Mobility Action Plan. Components of the Mobility Action Plan, such as completion of the Safe Routes to Schools program, traffic signal modernization, and construction of major bicycle and pedestrian infrastructure are costly and will necessitate development of enhanced funding sources. Similarly, components of the Climate Action Plan including electric vehicle charging infrastructure for City vehicles and converting City buildings from gas to electric heating call for major investments. Other new requirements, which are regulatory in nature, have increased dramatically over the last few years, and have added significant costs to City operations. The City’s Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Transition Plan is projected to need over $100 million over the next 25 years. Anticipating the slowdown in revenue growth for FY 2025/26 that we’re now experiencing, the adopted General Fund budget was balanced by reducing ongoing funding for capital maintenance activities by $3.2 million. Later in the year, the City Council approved additional ongoing reductions, totaling $3.1 million across all City departments, to offset higher personnel costs resulting from negotiated labor agreements. While the FY 2026/27 adopted General Fund operating budget contemplates no additional service reductions, the only increase in staffing is to add a position to provide administrative support for the Mayor and City Councilmembers. As noted in the key budget assumptions, because the City is engaged in labor negotiations, the adopted budget also includes a 2% placeholder salary adjustment. Budget Overview Major City Initiatives The City of Fremont continues to support and invest in major strategic growth initiatives while navigating an operating environment characterized by everchanging conditions and macroeconomic uncertainty. These initiatives are important elements of our diversified tax base strategy to preserve and expand Fremont’s General Fund over time and position the City for sustainable economic growth and fiscal stability. Development Fremont continues to experience strong development momentum, driven by sustained demand from advanced manufacturing, life sciences, clean energy, robotics, and AI hardware companies. Major private‑sector investments across key employment districts -- Warm Springs, Bayside, Pacific Commons, Ardenwood, and City Center -- are transforming former underutilized sites into high‑value employment campuses, mixed‑use destinations, and modern industrial facilities. Collectively, these projects generate significant job growth, attract emerging technologies, support vital infrastructure upgrades, and reinforce Fremont’s position as one of Silicon Valley’s most competitive markets for innovation, manufacturing, and long‑term economic expansion. Warm Springs Innovation District The Warm Springs Innovation District remains one of Fremont’s most strategically important employment centers, distinguished by its scale, transportation access to Warm Springs BART Station, I-680, SR-262, and I-880, and concentration of advanced manufacturing and technology firms. Spanning approximately 850 acres, the district offers a unique “blank canvas” environment large enough to support next‑generation industrial development while providing the infrastructure and land use protections necessary for high‑intensity production uses. Budget Overview Warm Springs continues to attract major employers in clean technology, semiconductors, robotics, energy storage, and biomedical production. Companies such as Tesla, Lam Research, Delta Products, Seagate, Western Digital, ThermoFisher, and Boston Scientific all maintain significant operations in the district. This clustering effect reinforces Fremont’s position as one of the nation’s most important hubs for advanced hardware manufacturing and integration. The district’s momentum is further highlighted by several major development projects. In 2025 the City celebrated the groundbreaking for the Fremont Innovation Center, a 70,000-plus-squarefoot advanced manufacturing facility that transforms a long-vacant commercial parcel into a new manufacturing site. Upon completion, the project is expected to generate more than 100 permanent high-tech jobs, contribute over $2 million in infrastructure funding, and activate a key strategic location. Meanwhile, 49000 Milmont Drive, completed in late 2025, is a 267,000-square-foot advanced manufacturing building now fully leased by Tesla for robotic manufacturing operations. This project further strengthens Warm Springs as a hub for high-tech employment and next-generation mobility innovation. Additionally, the Sobrato Warm Springs Advanced Manufacturing Campus is a proposed 22-acre master-planned development featuring 420,000 square feet of new manufacturing and R&D space expected to break ground in September 2026. Overall, the Warm Springs Innovation District continues to mature into a flagship employment hub, combining major private‑sector investment, high‑value industrial land uses, transformative infrastructure projects, and long‑term planning strategies that reinforce Fremont’s economic leadership in Silicon Valley. Bayside Technology Park Bayside Technology Park continues to reinforce its position as one of Fremont’s most active and strategically significant advanced manufacturing districts. With more than 20 million square feet of flexible R&D and industrial space and strong demand from global technology firms, Bayside remains a premier location for companies scaling production, R&D, semiconductor work, and AI‑driven technologies. As industrial demand accelerates -- fueled by reshoring manufacturing, the growth of AI hardware, and ongoing innovation across clean energy and biomedical sectors -Bayside plays a critical role in attracting high‑value investment to Fremont. A major highlight for Bayside is the groundbreaking of Phase 1 of Campus at Bayside, a 473,250‑square‑foot advanced manufacturing project located at 47100 Lakeview Boulevard. This Budget Overview project represents one of the largest industrial investments breaking ground in Silicon Valley in 2025. The development showcases Fremont’s competitive edge as a manufacturing hub and is expected to create up to 2,500 new manufacturing and R&D jobs at full build‑out. Phase 1 has already been fully pre-leased with the groundbreaking for Phase 2 in the pipeline. Prologis has acquired multiple strategic sites at the Siemens campus and is proposing a new 200,000‑square‑foot advanced manufacturing project, reinforcing their deep and long‑standing presence in Fremont’s industrial market. With this upcoming project, Prologis’ Fremont portfolio includes 55 buildings totaling 4.6 million square feet, with nearly all of this space leased to manufacturing and technology companies. A defining advantage for Bayside is the City’s collaboration with LS Power to bring major utility upgrades to the district. The $500 million “Power the Bay” project is connecting nearly 1 gigawatt of solar‑generated power to Fremont’s Bayside transmission station, with an associated 75-megawatt local grid distribution expansion to support advanced manufacturing growth. This transformative infrastructure investment also provides five miles of dedicated fiberoptic conduit to the City for future high‑speed broadband needs. Pacific Commons and Fremont Auto Mall The Pacific Commons area is a disproportionate driver of General Fund revenues for the City due to the sales tax revenues provided by the Fremont Auto Mall -- one of the largest auto malls in California -- and Pacific Commons Shopping Center, one of the largest outdoor shopping malls in the country. Fremont’s Auto Mall continues to show resiliency in the face of changing macroeconomic conditions, with new dealership franchises continuing to locate there. This includes Enterprise Mobility Solutions, which in 2025 opened a new 3‑in‑1 dealership, rental center, and commercial truck facility -- its largest dealership in California. In Pacific Commons Shopping Center, H Mart announced the purchase of a 100,000-square-foot former Kohl’s building, where it plans to build a flagship multi-level food and entertainment hub, its largest investment in company history. Immediately adjacent to the shopping center is Pacific Commons South. A 2.5 million-square-foot modern industrial development, Pacific Commons South continues to play a major role in Fremont’s economic growth, supporting job creation, industrial reinvestment, and new retail activity. The Budget Overview master-planned, 10-building campus is leased to many of the region’s leading technology companies, including Meta, Quanta Computer, Bloom Energy, UPS, and Amazon. Nearby, the recently developed, 400,000-square-foot Fremont Tech Center campus has reached full occupancy, generating approximately $4 million in one‑time impact fees and an estimated 650 full‑time jobs. It exemplifies Fremont’s ability to reposition former retail sites into high‑value employment centers. Ardenwood Technology Park Ardenwood Technology Park offers a more idyllic setting amongst Fremont’s industrial employment districts. Strategically located 2.5 miles from the Peninsula at the eastern landing of the Dumbarton Bridge, the district offers unmatched regional access -- providing a shorter or reverse commute for workers traveling from the Peninsula, South Bay, and the greater East Bay. Employers consistently cite Ardenwood’s central location and high‑quality campus environment as key advantages for scaling operations. Ardenwood is home to one of Fremont’s largest concentrations of biotechnology, life science, and advanced technology companies. Recent expansions include Meta, Nextpower, Novo Nordisk, Boehringer Ingelheim, and Alexza Pharmaceuticals, each deepening their manufacturing and R&D footprints in the district. With its combination of locational advantages, high‑value employers, flexible zoning, and access to world‑class amenities, Ardenwood Technology Park remains one of Fremont’s most competitive and future‑ready districts for biotechnology, clean energy, semiconductor, and office‑based innovation. Untapped development capacity still exists in Ardenwood, supported by greenfield sites and higher density zoning, which staff expect to materialize into new employment centers and General Fund revenues in the coming years. Downtown and City Center Downtown Fremont and the broader City Center area continue to evolve. Envisioned as Fremont’s primary gathering hub, this centrally located district is defined by its walkable street grid, proximity to regional transit, and concentration of civic, commercial, and residential uses. The 110‑acre Downtown Community Plan area, framed by Fremont Boulevard, Mowry Avenue, Paseo Padre Parkway, and Walnut Avenue, sits at the heart of the larger 430‑acre City Center Community Plan area, both of which provide the long‑term land use framework guiding Fremont’s downtown revitalization. Budget Overview The City has invested heavily in creating the foundation for a vibrant mixed‑use district. A walkable street grid with enhanced pedestrian linkages connects Downtown to the nearby Fremont BART Station, while public and private developments have delivered new urban amenities, civic spaces, and a growing mix of retail and residential opportunities. Within a one‑mile radius of Downtown, there are already 15,000 residents and a 20,000-person workforce primarily geared toward healthcare and retail, and the district benefits from adjacency to major commercial anchors including the Fremont Hub, Gateway Plaza, and Fremont Plaza shopping centers. Several transformative projects are shaping the next wave of Downtown and City Center growth: • The Hub and Gateway Plaza Redevelopment (Kimco Projects) Two significant redevelopment projects at The Hub and Gateway Plaza, led by Kimco Realty, were unanimously approved by the Planning Commission and later upheld by City Council. These projects will bring over 500 units of multifamily housing, new retail space, community amenities, and enhanced streetscapes -- transforming primarily surface‑parked shopping centers into mixed‑use anchors that strengthen Downtown’s commercial core. • Capitol Avenue and Capitol Square Capitol Avenue continues to serve as Downtown Fremont’s emerging “retail spine,” supported by strong retail leasing activity. In 2025, the Capitol Square development reached full “lease‑up” of its 11 ground-floor commercial spaces, reinforcing the burgeoning district’s capacity to attract small businesses, restaurants, wellness services, and locally owned shops. • Downtown Event Center (DTEC) The City‑owned Downtown Event Center, opened in 2021, has become a major event venue hosting thousands of attendees annually. It is a central activation hub for industry events and community gatherings. This facility supports both community programming and Downtown’s growing cultural identity. Budget Overview Downtown Fremont is one of the rare opportunities in the Bay Area to build a downtown from the ground up. Since the adoption of the Downtown Community Plan in 2012 and the City Center Community Plan in 2016, the area has seen: • A new civic plaza and event center • High‑density residential entitlement and construction activity • Growth in ground‑floor commercial tenants • New six-story office headquarters for Fremont Bank • Increasing interest in mixed‑use redevelopment of older commercial centers These developments collectively reinforce Downtown Fremont as a growing regional destination for living, working, shopping, and cultural activity. Business Attraction Fremont’s business attraction efforts continue to strengthen the City’s advanced industry ecosystem, drawing high‑growth companies across manufacturing, clean energy, life sciences, and next‑generation technology sectors. Through proactive outreach, real estate and permitting support, and close coordination with regional partners, the City helps companies expand and establish new operations in Fremont. This high‑touch, relationship‑driven approach supports job creation, innovation, and long‑term fiscal stability while reinforcing Fremont’s position as one of the Bay Area’s most competitive markets for industrial and technology investment. These activities contributed significantly to Fremont’s record‑setting year in 2025, during which the City led all Silicon Valley submarkets with nearly five million square feet of commercial space leased, and captured 70% of all advanced manufacturing leases in the Bay Area, reflecting its dominant position in the industrial and hardware technology sectors. Fremont supported significant expansions by leading firms such as AMAX, Bionova Scientific, Bloom Energy, Boehringer Ingelheim, Lam Research, Nextpower (formerly Nextracker), Novo Nordisk, Novo Pneuma (formerly Alexza Pharmaceuticals), Quanta Manufacturing, Raxium, TD Synnex, Tesla, Wisk Aero, and Wistron. These expansions represent some of the region’s most active and capital‑intensive industrial investments. Fremont also successfully attracted many fast‑growing and emerging companies in next‑generation technologies including Aivres, Agility Robotics, Avidex Industries, Kuprion, Stacked Energy, Tandem PV, and Mitac Information Systems. These companies selected Fremont for its advanced manufacturing ecosystem, workforce talent, and robust public‑private support infrastructure. Budget Overview Advanced Industry Sector Highlights Fremont continues to strengthen its role as a national hub for advanced industries, supported by major investments in biomedical manufacturing, clean energy, semiconductor technology, autonomous mobility, and AI‑driven hardware. The City’s business‑friendly environment, deep manufacturing expertise, and coordinated utility and permitting support create ideal conditions for companies scaling complex and power‑intensive production operations. The biomedical and life sciences sector remains one of Fremont’s fastest‑growing clusters, with more than 150 companies contributing to ongoing research and advanced manufacturing. Recent expansions by firms such as Bionova Scientific, Boehringer Ingelheim, and Novo Nordisk continue to deepen the city’s specialized talent base and reinforce long‑term stability through high‑skilled employment and production capacity. Clean‑energy and battery innovation also continue to accelerate, driven by companies that leverage Fremont’s industrial capabilities and infrastructure readiness. Bloom Energy and Stacked Energy are expanding clean‑energy and storage technology manufacturing across the city, while firms throughout the cleantech ecosystem benefit from federal incentives and Fremont’s strategic support for power‑intensive operations. Together, these investments bolster Fremont’s position as a national leader in energy‑transition technologies. Semiconductors, AI hardware, and high‑performance computing remain key pillars of Fremont’s advanced industry landscape. Semiconductor and related companies such as Nova Systems and Lam Research continue to grow their presence. Fremont has emerged as one of the country’s most important hubs for AI server and computing hardware. The City now hosts 33 AI server manufacturing facilities totaling approximately four million square feet -- one of the largest concentrations globally -- up from just six facilities three years ago. These companies collectively drive demand for power infrastructure, support next‑generation computing innovation, and enhance Fremont’s competitiveness in global technology supply chains. Retail and Commercial Vibrancy Retail and commercial vibrancy remain central pillars of Fremont’s economic development strategy, supporting both quality‑of‑life and the success of small businesses across the city. Through coordinated outreach, targeted programming, and strategic partnerships with property owners and brokers, the City continues to cultivate a vibrant retail ecosystem that strengthens Fremont’s neighborhood business districts, Downtown, and destination shopping areas. Budget Overview Downtown and City Center Retail Activity Downtown Fremont continues to evolve into a vibrant, walkable district supported by new ground‑floor commercial spaces and strong tenant activity. The City assisted numerous retailers with navigating opening requirements, helping to expand the district’s mix of food, beverage, wellness, and specialty retail offerings. New businesses in the City Center area include: Angry Chickz, Dosa Dash, Palmetto, Paradox Barbershop, Pints of Joy, Pizza My Heart, Pour Decisions, Shugetsu, Stardust, The Kebab Shop, Waxing the City, and Zaitoon. Downtown’s mixed‑use projects continue to show strong performance: • Capitol Square, Downtown’s first mixed‑use development, is fully leased with eleven local businesses, including Banter Bookshop, Paradox Barber Shop, and Din Ding Dumpling House. • The Beacon and The Tolman developments have activated their ground‑floor commercial spaces with businesses such as Pour Decisions, Waxing the City, and Palmetto Super Foods. The City also invests in placemaking events that bring thousands of visitors Downtown. Activations like the 2nd Annual Holidays at the Plaza, Downtown Dog Days, Downtown Dance, Fremont Restaurant Week, and other family‑friendly events collectively attracted more than 10,000 attendees, driving both foot traffic and economic activity for small businesses. Citywide Retail Vibrancy Commercial vibrancy is an important priority across Fremont’s neighborhoods beyond Downtown. In collaboration with property owners, retail brokers, and commercial managers, the City continues to support reinvestment and tenant attraction in key commercial corridors. Notable new retail openings citywide include: Bikanervala, Bintang, Bun Bun Chinese Food, Cassa Jam, Chicha San Chen, Extra Coffee Roasting Company, H Mart, Miniso, Qamaria Yemeni Coffee, Sourdough & Co., Umika Sushi, Wadaya, Wushiland Boba, and X20 Studios. The City also launched Access Fremont, a free high‑speed public Wi‑Fi initiative serving commercial districts. Introduced in October 2025, the program enhances visitors’ experience and supports small‑business operations across Fremont’s key retail nodes. Budget Overview Pacific Commons Retail Anchors and Major Investments Pacific Commons remains a major regional retail destination, bolstered by significant new anchor investments: • H Mart purchased a two‑story, 100,000‑square‑foot building to establish its largest California grocery store and its most substantial investment to date. The new flagship location will include dine‑in restaurants, a bar, live music, and a food hall experience. • Miniso celebrated the grand opening of its new flagship North America location at Pacific Commons -- its largest store outside of Asia -- showcasing the district’s ability to attract high‑profile global retailers. These anchor projects position Pacific Commons as a continued powerhouse for regional retail, complementing the district’s robust advanced manufacturing presence. Capital Projects The City has an ongoing Capital Improvement Program (CIP) that provides investments to improve infrastructure related to the City’s transportation system, parks, and building facilities. Primary funding for these investments comes from development impact fees; State gas taxes; County transportation funds; grants from federal, State, and regional sources; and ongoing and one-time transfers from the General Fund. In the recent past, significant projects completed include the West Access Bridge and Plaza at the Warm Springs BART Station and Dusterberry Neighborhood Park. Notable projects in construction include: • Central Park Community Center and Event Hall, a $51 million project planned for completion in Spring 2028. • Park Restroom Modernization Program, a multi-year program to replace or remodel 18 old park restrooms with project completions occurring in 2026 (eight locations), 2027 (six locations), and 2028 (four locations). • Vallejo Mill Historic Park Improvements, with a new dog park and pickle ball courts, is planned for completion in Spring 2026. • Electric Vehicle Charging for City Fleet Vehicles, providing an expansion of charging capacity at the Maintenance Center, Development Center, and City Hall, is planned for completion in Summer 2026. Looking ahead, the City’s past Capital Budget approvals and the adopted five-year CIP (FY 2025/26 through FY 2029/30) include projects and programs valued at $236 million. The highlights of planned projects and capital investments are as follows. Budget Overview Capital Maintenance Preservation and maintenance of existing City assets is a primary focus of the CIP. The highest level of funding in Capital Maintenance is allocated to ongoing annual projects to repave City streets, repair sidewalks, curbs and gutters in the worst condition, and build ADA curb ramps. This also includes maintenance and capital replacement funding for parks, landscaped median islands, street lighting, and buildings, as well as a 50/50 grant program to assist residents with sidewalk repairs and street tree replacements. Other funded projects include: • Buildings with aging heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) systems will have old natural gas units replaced with new electrical equipment, where feasible, and will align with Fremont’s clean energy goals. Projects planned for construction over the next three years include: Fire Stations 1, 4, 5, 7 and 10; Police Center dispatch center; Warm Springs and Centerville community centers; Centerville Library, and the Maintenance Center office building. • Historic buildings planned for new roof systems include the Centerville Train Depot (2026), Chadbourne Carriage House (2026), and Patterson House (2027). • Planning for replacing approximately 16,000 LED streetlights citywide to ensure replacement before they reach the end of their expected life. It is noted that $3.2 million of annual funding from the General Fund for pavement maintenance and parks capital replacement was eliminated beginning in FY 2025/26 which is expected to result in a decline in pavement conditions and delayed replacement of aging parks infrastructure. Transportation The Transportation CIP includes investments for traffic operations and signal system improvement, bicycle and pedestrian facilities, and major projects. • Investments in traffic operations and signal projects include annual expenditures to maintain existing traffic signals, modernize equipment for more efficient operations, construct new traffic signals at priority locations to improve safety, and to respond to community interests/concerns related to traffic operations. • The City receives dedicated funds from the County Measure BB program and State grants for “complete streets” projects to enable better travel opportunities for walking and bicycling. This program helps deliver priority projects identified in the City’s updated Active Transportation Plan and Safe Routes to Schools program. • A significant element of the City’s Transportation CIP is oriented toward major and regional projects. This includes the City’s support for developing the new Irvington BART Station; connecting communities with trails by building bridges over freeways in the I-880/Innovation and I-680/Sabercat areas; and modernizing freeway interchanges at I-680/Mission and I-880/ Decoto. In addition, the City has been approved to receive $62 million in grant funding for multimodal transportation projects in the Dumbarton/Decoto corridor, the Peralta/Mowry corridor, and the Fremont Boulevard corridor. Budget Overview Parks and Recreation The Parks CIP includes investments to implement the Parks and Recreation Master Plan adopted by the City Council in March 2022. Significant projects to enhance parks and recreation programs in Fremont include the following: • Centerville Community Park Expansion, increasing the park size from 10 to 20 acres, with construction planned to start in Summer 2026. This expansion will include a new playground, group and individual picnic areas, large and small field areas, and a new parking lot to accommodate added users. Four pickleball courts, adult exercise equipment, and three bocce ball courts will expand and diversify Fremont’s non-youth offerings. • Palm Avenue Community Park project will develop 12 acres of park in a currently park-deficient area of Fremont. With the opening of this park, approximately 2,700 people will have new access to a public park within a ten-minute walk of their homes, moving Fremont closer to its goal of improved park equity. • The Parks CIP also funds other ongoing projects for improvements such as new ADA upgrades, benches, and trails to add pathways and benches to existing parks, in alignment with other City efforts, such as the Age-Friendly Fremont Action Plan. Legislative Advocacy The City continues to be proactive with its legislative advocacy efforts and has forged ahead with building partnerships at the federal, State, and regional levels to ensure the interests and concerns of Fremont and the region are preserved. The City’s Legislative Framework, approved by the City Council, establishes guiding principles and priorities, and serves as the City’s foundation for pursuing major initiatives and funding opportunities. Adopting a legislative framework enables City staff and lobbyists to actively advocate for, influence, and monitor State and federal legislation that best represents Fremont’s interests. The City Council held its annual retreat in February 2026 to establish four priority policy areas for the City in FY 2026/27, which included (1) Economic Development and Financial Sustainability, (2) Reduce Homelessness, (3) Public Safety, and (4) Charter City Initiative. The City’s legislative advocacy efforts for FY 2026/27 will focus on addressing these priorities. Budget Overview Economic Development and Fiscal Sustainability Continue to strengthen Fremont’s economic competitiveness and long-term fiscal health by prioritizing strategic business attraction and retention, workforce development, and targeted investments that enhance Downtown vibrancy. Align economic development, community identity, and quality-of-life initiatives with long-term budget sustainability, while establishing measurable outcomes that can be clearly communicated to community and stakeholders. Reduce homelessness Build on progress and strengthen outcome orientation in Fremont’s homelessness response. Emphasize coordinated strategies that connect housing availability, service delivery, and measurable outcomes such as outreach effectiveness, shelter placements, navigation capacity, and transitions to stable housing. Strengthen regional coordination and public transparency regarding results and challenges. Public safety Sustain and enhance public safety staffing and service capacity, while improving how public safety trends, strategies, and outcomes are communicated to the community. Continue to support recruitment and retention and reinforce public confidence through transparent, data-driven reporting and engagement. Charter City Framework This priority reflects the Council’s direction to initiate a structured work plan to evaluate the option of a City Charter, including the formation of an advisory committee and coordination with City staff to support analysis and public engagement. The intent of this work program is to conduct the evaluation and associated community engagement in a manner that would position a Charter City proposal for potential placement on the November 2026 ballot, subject to Council review and consideration as the evaluation proceeds. During the California State Legislature’s 2025 Legislative Cycle, the Governor signed more than 700 bills into law. Some of the themes/topics addressed at the Legislature in 2025 included education, labor/workforce, transportation, infrastructure, environment, health and social services, housing, public safety, and local government administration/operations. At the national level, in 2025, the United States Convened for the 1st session of the 119th Congress, and the Trump administration succeeded the Biden administration. This change brought new leadership across various federal agencies and shifts in federal policies to reflect the new administration’s priorities. Notably, in 2025, the President signed H.R. 1 (One Big Beautiful Bill Act) into law, which included a series of provisions relating to taxes and various federal programs, as well as increasing the statutory debt limit. Other major legislative developments at Congress included S. 2651 (ROAD to Housing Act) and H.R. 4669 (FEMA Act of 2025), among others. Heading into the 2026 Legislative Cycle, City staff will monitor and review bills and regulatory changes that affect our community and local economy. Budget Overview In 2025, Congressman Ro Khanna advocated to help secure $850,000 in federal Community Project Funding for the City’s Auto Mall Parkway Center Median Project, which was ultimately included in a consolidated appropriations package for FY 2026 that the President signed into law in February 2026. Further, in March 2026, Congressman Eric Swalwell submitted the City’s Lake Elizabeth Improvement Project ($3 million) and the Traffic Safety Improvement Project at Dusterberry Community Park ($3 million) for FY 2027 Community Project Funding. Additionally, Congressman Ro Khanna submitted the City’s Hetch-Hetchy Trail Gap Closure Project at Scott Creek Road ($3 million) and Walnut Avenue to Dixon Landing Road Quiet Zone Corridor Project ($4 million) for FY 2027 Community Project Funding. City staff will continue to monitor the progress of these funding requests, and will seek additional regional, state, and federal funding opportunities to further advance the City’s priority objectives. Over the next year, staff will continue to work with our legislative advocates to prioritize and track legislation, while continuously evaluating the legislative climate to identify new areas of opportunity, with the overarching goal of improving quality of life and creating an equitable future for all, consistent with the City’s vision, goals, and policies Conclusion Fremont prides itself on being a fiscally responsible, lean organization, making the most of the resources entrusted to us. This adopted budget focuses our limited ongoing revenues on the most essential City services while continuing to defer certain maintenance activities. To the extent additional resources become available, we will work to ensure that they are used to address the City Council’s and community’s highest priorities. I would like to thank both the City Council and City staff for the strong partnership that will carry us through these challenging times. RT Line, ention, Majo BART Line Ext Fremont’s rich heritage can be traced to the Ohlones, natives of the land, and to the Spanish priests who established Mission San Jose, the first Spanish mission located inland. Since those early days, Fremont’s rich soil, central location, and excellent climate have continued to attract newcomers to this area. In the mid-1840s, John C. Fremont mapped a trail through Mission Pass to provide access for American settlers into the southeastern San Francisco Bay Area. During the Gold Rush era, the Mission area attracted miners headed for the California gold fields. Governor Leland Stanford acquired land in the Warm Springs area, where he planted vineyards and built one of the first wineries in the state. The Niles district made history when the last tracks needed to connect the transcontinental railroad were laid there. Further acclaim came to Niles when Charlie Chaplin filmed “The Tramp” at the Essanay Movie Studio there. In 1853, Washington Township was established and included the communities of Mission San Jose, Centerville, Niles, Irvington, and Warm Springs. On January 23, 1956, these communities joined to form the City of Fremont. Summary Information | City of Fremont Profile Council Districts . Ma yor tr erm. Fremont, located in southern Alameda County, stretches from the San Francisco Bay to the top of Mission Peak above historic Mission San Jose in the east. With a population of 233,974, Fremont is the fourth largest city in the San Francisco Bay Area and ranks in the top 100 among the most populous cities in the nation according to the US Census Bureau. Fremont is approximately 92 square miles in size and includes the 450-acre Central Park and 80-acre Lake Elizabeth, along with 64 other parks, six community centers, and extensive sports facilities. Fremont is also home to the Don Edwards San Francisco Bay National Wildlife Refuge, adjacent to Coyote Hills Regional Park. Fremont enjoys a high rate of home ownership, a low crime rate, and a quality of life that is considered to be one of the best in the United States. For example, Fremont was rated number one in the nation for Happiest City by WalletHub in a national study that compared large cities across three key dimensions: 1) Emotional and Physical Well-Being, 2) Income and Employment and 3) Community and Environment. Fremont residents enjoy a highly rated public education system, low crime rates, and a vast array of recreation, park, and other leisure activities. In addition to beautiful parks and extensive recreational facilities, Fremont has easy access to three international airports, several major educational institutions, the Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART) system, and professional sports and cultural opportunities. Fremont is also home to Washington Hospital, a community asset for over 50 years. Population: 233,974 Elevation: 56 feet City of Fremont logo. Summary Information | All City Funds Schedule All City Funds Schedule The Summary of All Funds schedule on the following page groups the City’s funds into four categories: • General Fund • Cost Center/Internal Service • Special Revenue • Capital The first three categories include the City’s operating funds, and the last one is a special purpose fund used for capital investments. Funding for most of the City’s operations and most of its services comes from the first three fund categories. The budget for Capital funds is reviewed and adopted by the City Council as part of the Capital Improvement Program (CIP). The Summary of All Funds schedule consolidates all funds citywide and presents the total available resources and total use of resources, including beginning fund balances, revenues, expenditures, “transfers in,” and “transfers out.” This consolidation is achieved by eliminating all transfers between funds that are within the same fund category and all internal service fund charge transfers. Such eliminations are similar to those made to produce the City’s government-wide financial statements, as mandated by Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB) Statement 34. These eliminations avoid the double counting that would otherwise occur if these transactions were shown as either additional transfers or as additional revenues and expenditures. Therefore, the “Total Revenues” and “Total Expenditures” lines for all funds present the true budgeted revenues and expenditures expected to be received and spent by the entire organization. Please refer to the General Fund section and the Other Funds section of this document for more information. equivalent (FTE) positions from the FY 2025/26 level. Reflecting lower volumes of development activity and constrained resources, the City has reduced staffing over the last several years, and many departments continue to operate at a low level when compared to historical staffing ratios. The Human Services Department staffing decrease of 2.8 positions is a consequence of Alameda County Behavior Health (ACBH) defunding its $1.25 million mental health contract as of June 30, 2026. Since 2008, ACBH has contracted with the City to provide a number of senior-focused programs and services funded through the Mental Health Services Act (MHSA). In March 2024, California voters passed Proposition 1, which will supplant the MHSA and result in a loss of $1.25 million for Fremont’s Senior Mental Health Program. The City Council staff increase represents the addition of one Administrative Analyst to provide administrative support for the Mayor and City Councilmembers. General obligation (GO) bonds are secured by the City’s obligation to annually levy ad valorem taxes on all taxable properties within the City in an amount necessary to pay debt service. Following voter approval in 2002, GO bonds were issued in 2003, 2005, and 2009 to build or improve City public safety facilities. The 2003 GO bonds were refunded with the issuance of the 2012 General Obligation Refunding Bonds, the 2005 GO bonds were refunded with the issuance of the 2013 General Obligation Refunding Bonds, and the 2009 GO bonds were refunded with the issuance of the 2017 General Obligation Refunding Bonds. The 2012 General Obligation Refunding Bonds and 2013 General Obligation Refunding Bonds were refunded with the issuance of the 2021 General Obligation Refunding Bonds. General Fund Bonds (Lease Revenue Bonds). Lease revenue bonds entitle investors to receive payments from an underlying financing lease between the City and the Fremont Public Financing Authority. The Authority uses the lease revenue received from the City to pay principal and interest on the lease obligations. The City has two outstanding series of lease revenue bonds: the 2017B Lease Revenue Bonds and the 2019 Lease Revenue Bonds, which were issued to finance or refinance the acquisition or construction of various capital assets including building improvements and fire equipment. The 2017B Lease Revenue Bonds were defeased (pre-paid into an escrow fund) in April 2023. Although the City is no longer responsible for the principal and interest payments on the 2017B Bonds, escrow agent and paying agent fees will be budgeted until the bonds are redeemed on October 1, 2027. The 2019 Bonds bear interest at fixed rates. The lease payments and associated financing costs are payable from the General Fund, although a portion of the lease payments associated with the 2019 Bonds are paid from rental revenue of tenants at the Fremont Family Resource Center. Standard & Poor’s maintains ratings of AA+ (stable outlook) on the City’s general obligation bonds and AA (stable outlook) on its lease revenue bonds. In brief, the City’s appropriations growth rate is limited to changes in population and either the change in California per capita income or the change in the local assessment roll due to new, nonresidential construction. The formula to be used in calculating the growth factor is: multiplied by either: or The resultant factor times the previous appropriations limit equals the new appropriation limit. Both the California per capita personal income price factor and the population percentage change factor are provided by the State Department of Finance to local jurisdictions each year. The population percentage change factor estimates the change in the City’s population between January of the previous fiscal year and January of the current fiscal year. Reports that present changes in new non-residential assessed value are provided by the County of Alameda. Of the two methods above, the City is using the “per capita personal income” factor because it results in the higher appropriations limit. Summary Information | Citywide Goals and Objectives Citywide Goals and Objectives The City Council adopted a Strategic Plan that outlines a vision for the long-term future of Fremont and proposes strategies and short-term goals for achieving the vision. The plan has three main purposes. First, it communicates the City’s vision for the future to residents, businesses, and City employees. Second, it provides guidance so that decisions are good for today’s challenges and good for the City in the future. Making decisions in the context of a shared vision developed through collaboration ensures broad commitment to the success of the plan. Finally, the Strategic Plan provides a sound framework for long-term departmental planning. For budgeting purposes, the long-term desired outcomes and values outlined in the plan have been adopted as citywide goals that support the City Council’s vision. The goals are used as a framework for ensuring alignment of department objectives with the City Council’s vision. This section of the budget document presents the City Council’s vision and goals. It also includes a matrix that illustrates the alignment of departmental objectives with citywide goals. Department objectives presented here may be abbreviated for format purposes. text: City Council, Boards, and Commissions work with the community to create the long-term vision for Fremont and provide policy direction and guidance to the City organization. In Fremont, residents work together and with City staff to prevent crime and solve problems in their neighborhoods. The local economy is comprised of a strong, diversified commercial and industrial base, providing high-quality employment for the region. It is balanced with a strong retail sector and healthy neighborhood commercial districts. Summary Information | Citywide Goals and Objectives resources The City values a harmonious blend of natural and physical environments, with particular priority for preservation of open space, such as the hillface and bay wetlands. Quality of life is highly dependent on high quality transportation systems, which enable people to get around easily. Alternatives to automobile transportation, such as walking, cycling, and public transit are also valued. Public facilities provide individual and family entertainment, relaxation, and education. Proposition 13, adopted by California voters on June 6, 1978, created a comprehensive system for the assessment and limitation of real property taxes. Property owners pay the tax based on their real property’s adjusted assessed full value. Proposition 13 set the FY 1975/76 assessed values as the base year from which future annual inflationary assessed value increases would grow (not to exceed 2% for any given year). The County Assessor also reappraises each real property parcel when there are changes in ownership or new construction. The County Assessor may also temporarily reduce a property’s assessed value if the market value falls below the Proposition 13 level (often referred to as a “Proposition 8” adjustment), but is required to restore the Proposition 13 assessment in subsequent years if the market value increases to that level or above. Proposition 13 limits the property tax rate to 1% of each property’s full value plus overriding rates to pay voters’ specifically approved indebtedness The City of Fremont receives approximately 15 cents of every dollar of property tax paid. Alameda County and the schools, including Fremont Unified School District, receive most of the revenue from property taxes assessed on property located in the City Forecast: Property tax revenues are estimated to total $152.5 million in FY 2025/26. General Fund | General Fund Revenues Franchise Fees Description: State law provides cities with the authority to grant franchises to privately-owned utility and other companies for their use of the public right-of-way. The City receives franchise fees from the electric and gas utility, the solid waste collection company, local cable companies, and certain other entities for the privilege of using the public right-of-way within the City. The dominant franchise fees are calculated as a percentage of the respective franchisee’s gross revenues (subject to specified statutory adjustments) earned from services delivered or performed by the franchisee within the City. The maximum gas and electric franchise rate is the greater of 1% on gas and electric adjusted gross revenues or 2% of the asset investment base within the City, as set by California law. PG&E pays its electric and gas utility franchise fee annually in April based on its revenues for the preceding calendar year. Gas and electric utility franchise revenues for FY 2026/27 will likely be computed as 1% of PG&E’s adjusted gross revenues for calendar year 2026 (the 1% of revenues method generally results in a greater fee than the 2% of invested assets method) and will be received by the City in April 2027. In addition to the rate applied to PG&E gross revenues, a surcharge on gas and electricity consumption is charged to customers using other energy providers. As East Bay Community Energy is the primary energy provider for Fremont residents and businesses, just over 32% of the total electric franchise fee revenues are captured through the surcharge. The solid waste collection franchise fees are negotiated between the City and the refuse collector. Cable providers operate under a state franchise, rather than a local franchise. The cable franchise rate, 5% of the cable company’s “gross revenues,” is established in accordance with AB 2987, the Digital Infrastructure Video Competition Act (DIVCA). The solid waste collection franchise fee is paid monthly and the cable franchise fee is paid quarterly (both in arrears) throughout the fiscal year. In March 2026, the City Council approved a franchise agreement with LS Power in connection with the regional Power the South Bay transmission line project. Under the agreement, LS Power will pay the City an annual fee in the range of 2.0% - 2.3% of the Fremont portion of its gross revenue on an annual basis. Forecast: The projected FY 2026/27 franchise fees revenue of $14.0 million represents an increase of 4.1% from the FY 2025/26 estimate of $13.4 million. Key Factors in the Forecast: Key factors affecting the major franchises are discussed below. • Electricity franchise: PG&E franchise fee revenues change because of changes to the cost of natural gas and other resources used to generate electricity, consumer power demands (which are affected by the economy), interstate energy contract pricing, and State and federal regulatory changes. PG&E franchise fee revenue for FY 2025/26 is $5.3 million, a 5.4% decrease from the prior year. The forecast assumes that the City’s gas and electricity franchise fees will increase by 6.1% in FY 2026/27 to $5.7 million, reflecting the ten-year average. • Cable franchise: AB 2987 was signed into California law and became effective January 1, 2007. This legislation transferred the franchising functions to the state and set a fixed franchise fee of 5%. Based on collections through April, the FY 2025/26 estimate is $1.1 million. The estimate reflects a 5.2% decrease from the prior year. The FY 2026/27 projection of just under $1.1 million assumes a 5.9% reduction, consistent with the trend over the last ten years. The decline in this category is the result of consumer shifts toward television access technologies which are not subject to the franchise fee. • Solid waste collection franchise: Solid waste collection (“garbage”) franchise fee revenues are estimated at $6.9 million in FY 2025/26, with a projected increase in FY 2026/27 of 4.3% for revenue of $7.2 million. Solid waste rate increases typically occur every other year, in even years, with the next increase occurring in January 2028. With an increased focus on recycling (which is not subject to franchise fees), new revenue growth will likely be coming primarily from fee increases and new development adding to the customer base. General Fund | General Fund Forecast General Fund Forecast The General Fund forecast is a planning tool that helps staff identify important trends and anticipate the longer-term consequences of budget decisions. The forecast has been instrumental in modeling the effects of such recent budget issues as rising retirement system costs, application of fiscal recovery funds, and potential scenarios for future revenue performance. The ability to model cost and revenue trends beyond the next budget year helps the City identify service levels that can be sustained through all phases of the business cycle. The forecast is not a plan, but a scenario based on revenue and cost assumptions that are updated regularly as new information becomes available. Of these components, future cost projections, based on known costs, are relatively reliable. Revenue forecasts, on the other hand, are based on assumptions related to future economic conditions, which are fraught with uncertainty. Economic forecasts reported in the media frequently swing from optimistic to pessimistic and demonstrate the perils of committing to a specific prediction of the future. For this reason, the forecast is updated regularly and is the subject of periodic City Council discussion. The key forecast assumptions are as follows: • The California consumer price index (CCPI) will increase by at least 2% during the forecast period, allowing assessed values to increase by at least 2% for FY 2027/28 and FY 2028/29. Added value from changes in property ownership is expected to remain low in calendar year 2026, affecting FY 2027/28 revenue growth, and then increase during 2027. New construction activity will further add to the property tax roll, but at the lower levels we’ve experienced recently. • Consistent with the underlying growth in sales tax revenue we’re experiencing in FY 2025/26, consumers and business will maintain their current purchasing behavior and annual growth of 3% will continue over the remainder of the forecast period. • Business tax and hotel/motel tax are projected to increase at their long-term averages of 3.5% and 5% respectively. • The placeholder salary adjustment of 2% included in the FY 2026/27 adopted budget is assumed to be part of a three-year agreement. Accordingly, additional 2% adjustments are included in the two forecast years. • Estimated pension contribution increases related to changes in investment earnings and assumptions have been incorporated based on information from CalPERS. Per the City Council Pension Liability Funding Policy, additional unfunded liability contributions have been included in FY 2026/27 and FY 2027/28, subject to City Council review. • Commitments for all scheduled debt service costs are included. • Annual transfers for maintenance and ADA projects will continue at the FY 2026/27 adopted budget level of $3.8 million. These funds receive revenues from external users in the form of fees for services and transfers from other funds for work on City projects. The cost centers are intended to maintain their fund balances from year to year to provide flexibility to respond to revenue decreases or unexpected costs. The City uses internal service funds to account for City-wide support services, such as risk management, information technology, and employee benefits, that operate on a cost-reimbursement basis, and to accumulate funds for vehicle, fire apparatus, and technology infrastructure capital replacement. Development Cost Center The Development Cost Center budget relies on a combination of development fees, charges to City capital projects, and charges to the General Fund (made in the form of a transfer) for work benefiting the community in general. In FY 2026/27, the General Fund will transfer $3.3 million to the Development Cost Center, to be allocated among the Planning, Engineering, and the Park Planning and Design Divisions to support their work programs. The work funded by the General Fund allocation generally includes updating and maintaining the City’s General Plan and Zoning Ordinance, implementing the Climate Action Plan, responding to traffic service requests, providing general customer service not associated with a particular project, and responding to City Council referrals. Other Funds | Cost Centers and Internal Service Funds The City Council has established a Development Cost Center operational contingency reserve to help maintain service levels during temporary slowdowns in development activity, as well as a technology and system improvement reserve to provide funding for investments in permitting technology. The Development Cost Center also collects a Community Planning Fee to recover a portion of the costs associated with the annual maintenance and comprehensive updates to the General Plan and Zoning Ordinance. The Community Planning Fee is assessed on each building permit plan checked and issued. At the end of FY 2026/27, the unreserved fund balance is projected to be $10.5 million. Recreation Cost Center The Recreation Cost Center provides services to the public through user fees and General Fund support. Employing an enterprise business model in which new programs are funded only if they are able to pay for themselves through fees, the Recreation Division successfully delivers programs and activities each year to citizens of all ages. Expanded programming, strong customer service, increased participation due to marketing efforts, and cost saving strategies have enabled the City to build a diverse and self-supporting portfolio of recreational offerings. In FY 2026/27, the Recreation Cost Center expects to receive 76.1% of its $13.0 million in ongoing resources from program and user fees, with 23.9% coming from state grant, other revenue, and investment income. The City Council has established a Recreation Cost Center contingency reserve to help maintain service levels during economic downturns or address revenue shortfalls. The contingency reserve requirement is set at 15% of annual operating expenditures and will be established at $1.8 million for FY 2026/27. Additional reserves include a $1.3 million equipment reserve and a $1.0 million operating improvement reserve that were established to reinvest back into future cost center business operations. For FY 2026/27, the Recreation Cost Center is projected to end the year with a $3.2 million unreserved fund balance. Senior Center Cost Center This cost center accounts for revenues and expenditures for programs administered by the Aging and Family Services (AFS) Division of the Human Services Department for the City’s two age well centers and other senior programs. Senior Center Cost Center resources are comprised of fees for service, restricted grants, private donations, and transfers in from the General Fund. Unlike other cost centers, the Senior Center Cost Center relies on General Fund support for the majority of its funding. In FY 2026/27, the amount of General Fund support for the Senior Center Cost Center will be $1.2 million, 2% more than the FY 2025/26 budget. Staff have responded to funding challenges over the last several years with a combination of fee increases, service reductions, fundraising, and use of reserves. Staff will continue to analyze Senior Center operations for opportunities to increase ongoing non-General Fund revenues and reduce operating costs to ensure long-term sustainability. Administrative costs, including workers’ compensation and general liability excess insurance coverage, are also accounted for in this fund. Resources for this fund are provided through direct allocation “charges” to the departments and special revenue fund operations that receive these services. Total costs allocated to departments will be $14.7 million in FY 2026/27. Information Technology Services Internal Service Fund This fund accounts for the City’s information systems support and technology services. It funds Information Technology Services operations and equipment replacement. Resources for this fund are provided through direct allocation “charges” to the departments and special revenue fund operations that receive these services. Total direct allocation charges to departments will be $19.1 million in FY 2026/27 for information technology services operations and various capital replacement purchases and software upgrades. The expenditure budget for this fund is increasing by $4.5 million from the adopted FY 2025/26 budget. This increase is primarily due to one-time capital expenditures, including a new emergency dispatch system for the Police Department. Employee Benefits Internal Service Fund In FY 2015/16, the city began prefunding its obligations for other post-employment healthcare benefits by annually prepaying the actuarially determined contribution to the CalPERS California Employers’ Retiree Benefit Trust (CERBT). This internal service fund accumulates contributions from each of the City’s operating funds and accounts for the payments to the CERBT, benefit payments to retirees, and reimbursements from the CERBT for those benefit payments. In FY 2026/27, the budgeted contribution to the CERBT for retiree healthcare is $9.0 million. During FY 2022/23, the City Council used General Fund surplus revenue to establish a reserve for unfunded accrued leave liabilities in the Employee Benefits Fund. This reserve is used to pay accrued leave balances when employees retire or terminate employment, or as part of an annual leave cash-out. For FY 2026/27, the estimated accrued leave inflow from the operating departments is $2.2 million and the budgeted payments are $2.2 million. This fund accumulates annual contributions from each of the City’s operating funds based on assigned vehicles, and accounts for the associated vehicle replacement purchases. Vehicle replacement contributions from all funds for FY 2026/27 are budgeted to total $2.3 million. To facilitate timely replacement of these critical capital assets, this fund accumulates annual contributions from the General Fund and accounts for the associated capital expenditures. The FY 2026/27 contribution from the General Fund is budgeted at $1.6 million.
